problemText: Which group of words is a sentence fragment? A fragment is missing a subject, a verb, or a finished thought.
choices: It was dark after the storm hit.
The storm knocked out the power.
The power went out during the storm.
Because the storm knocked out the power.
hints: Does this group have both a subject and a verb? Look for the starter word.
A word like because leaves you waiting for what happens next.

problemText: Read this sentence: "We wanted to go outside, it was raining too hard." What is the name of this error?
choices: Comma splice — two complete sentences joined with only a comma.
Run-on — two complete sentences connected with no punctuation mark between them at all.
Fragment — a sentence that is missing either a subject or a verb, making it incomplete.
Fragment — an incomplete sentence that lacks a finished thought or independent clause.
hints: Test each side of the comma separately. Does each side have a subject, a verb, and a finished thought?
This error happens when a comma is not strong enough to hold apart two complete sentences.

problemText: Which sentence is written correctly?
choices: After the bell rang loudly everyone jumped from their seats.
After the bell rang loudly, everyone jumped from their seats.
After the bell rang loudly. Everyone jumped from their seats.
After the bell rang loudly, the noise was very startling.
hints: When a starter word group comes first, it must attach to the complete sentence after it with a comma.
Check whether the words after the starter word can stand alone as a complete sentence.

problemText: Read this pair of sentences. "The cafeteria ran out of chocolate milk. Some students grabbed orange juice instead." Which revision uses a joining word to show the connection between these two complete sentences?
choices: The cafeteria ran out of chocolate milk; some students grabbed orange juice instead.
The cafeteria ran out of chocolate milk, some students grabbed orange juice instead.
The cafeteria ran out of chocolate milk, so some students grabbed orange juice instead.
Although the cafeteria ran out of chocolate milk, some students grabbed orange juice instead.
hints: A joining word like for, and, nor, but, or, yet, or so connects two complete sentences with a comma.
Which choice shows WHY the students grabbed orange juice instead?

problemText: Which sentence contains a fragment that needs to be fixed?
choices: The game was cancelled. Everyone went home disappointed.
Since the game was cancelled, everyone went home disappointed.
The game was cancelled, so everyone went home disappointed.
Since the game was cancelled everyone went home disappointed.
hints: Look for a starter word like since, because, although, or when that opens the sentence.
If a starter-word group comes first, does it have a comma after it before the complete sentence begins?

problemText: A student wrote: "We finished the project on time although we started late, everyone praised our work." Identify the error and choose the best correction.
choices: This is a comma splice. Fix it by adding a semicolon after the first complete thought: "We finished the project on time, although we started late; everyone praised our work."
This is a fragment. Fix it by removing the comma and adding a period: "We finished the project on time although we started late. Everyone praised our work."
This is a run-on error. Fix it by replacing the comma with a period: "We finished the project on time although we started late. Everyone praised our work."
This is a run-on with a misplaced dependent clause. Fix it by moving the starter word: "Although we started late, we finished the project on time, everyone praised our work."
hints: Test both parts after the comma in the original. Each side of a comma in the middle of a sentence must be part of one complete thought, not two separate ones.
A starter word like although belongs with the sentence idea it opens, not between two complete sentences.

problemText: What does it mean when a paragraph has sentence variety? A) The sentences are all the same length and use the same opener. B) The sentences mix different lengths and different opening words instead of repeating the same pattern. C) Some sentences are correct and some are fragments. D) The sentences use fancy or complicated words.
choices: The sentences mix different lengths and different opening words instead of repeating the same pattern.
The sentences are all the same length and use the same opener or subject at the beginning of each one.
Some sentences are correct and some contain fragments or incomplete thoughts.
The sentences use fancy or complicated vocabulary words to make the writing sound more advanced.
hints: Look for the definition taught in the lesson: what is sentence variety, and what does it NOT change?
Sentence variety changes the shape of sentences, not the facts. What pattern does it avoid?

problemText: Read these sentences: "The storm started. The lights flickered. The wind howled." What repeated pattern makes this paragraph sound choppy?
choices: Every sentence begins with the same subject or uses a repeated opening word pattern throughout the paragraph.
The first word of each sentence is exactly the same or a repeated subject.
All three sentences describe actions that happen at approximately the same moment in time.
Each sentence contains a strong action verb that shows something moving or changing.
hints: The lesson says the most noticeable repeated pattern is what? Look at the first word or subject of each sentence.
Compare the opening words: 'The storm,' 'The lights,' 'The wind.' What repeats?

problemText: Which revision of these two sentences adds a connector that states their relationship without changing what happened? Original: "The coach blew the whistle. The team sprinted toward the field." A) The coach blew the whistle and the team sprinted toward the field. B) The coach loudly blew the whistle, and the team sprinted toward the field. C) When the coach blew the whistle, the team sprinted toward the field. D) The coach blew the whistle. The team sprinted fast toward the field.
choices: The coach loudly blew the whistle, and the team sprinted toward the field.
The coach blew the whistle and the team sprinted toward the field.
When the coach blew the whistle, the team sprinted toward the field.
The coach blew the whistle. The team sprinted fast toward the field.
hints: A connector is a word such as when, after, because, or so. Which choice adds one of these words to state how the two events are related?
The whistle-blowing caused the team to sprint. Which word makes that timing relationship clear?

problemText: Read this paragraph: "Maya found her phone. Maya saw a text from her friend. Maya called her friend back. Maya talked for twenty minutes." To fix the choppy rhythm by removing the repeated opener and combining related sentences, which revision works best? A) Maya found her phone and saw a text from her friend, then called her back and talked for twenty minutes. B) Maya's phone, which had a text, led her to call and talk. C) Maya found her phone, Maya saw a text, and Maya called her friend back after she talked to her. D) Maya found her phone while seeing a text from her friend and calling her back to talk.
choices: Maya found her phone while seeing a text from her friend and calling her back to talk.
Maya's phone, which had a text, led her to call and talk.
Maya found her phone, Maya saw a text, and Maya called her friend back after she talked to her.
Maya found her phone and saw a text from her friend, then called her back and talked for twenty minutes.
hints: Count the repeated 'Maya' openers in the original. Which choice removes that repetition and keeps all four facts?
The lesson says a real fix removes a repeated opening word or adds a connector. Does this choice do at least one?

problemText: A student writes: "The final bell rang. Everyone packed their bags. The hallways filled with students." The student wants to fix the choppy rhythm. Which statement correctly describes what this revision does? Revision: "When the final bell rang, everyone packed their bags and the hallways filled with students." A) It adds a connector that states the timing relationship and combines related sentences to remove repetition. B) It makes the sentences longer by adding more descriptive words. C) It changes when the bell rang from first to last in time order. D) It removes the repeated opener and changes what happened to make it more interesting.
choices: It adds a connector that states the timing relationship and combines related sentences to remove repetition.
It joins multiple short sentences into fewer longer sentences by adding extra adjectives and detailed descriptions.
It rearranges the order of events so the bell rings last instead of at the beginning of the sequence.
It keeps the repeated subject but eliminates the choppy feeling by introducing additional characters and plot details.
hints: What two testable things fix a choppy rhythm? Does this revision do both, or just one?
Look at the word 'When' and at how many separate sentences the revision makes from the original three.

problemText: A writer submits this passage for the school yearbook: "The auditorium doors opened. The audience filled every seat. The lights dimmed. The curtain rose slowly. The orchestra began to play." The writer asks a peer, "How should I fix the choppy feel?" The peer suggests, "Make the sentences much longer and use bigger words." Is the peer's advice a real fix for sentence variety? Why or why not?
choices: Yes, because when you replace common words with more sophisticated vocabulary and expand each sentence to include additional descriptive details, the passage automatically sounds smoother and more polished.
No, because making sentences longer or using fancier words does not remove a repeated opening word or add a connector that states a relationship.
Yes, because combining all the short sentences into fewer, longer sentences by adding conjunctions like "and" between independent clauses will create the sense of flow and variety the writer wants.

No, because the choppiness comes from repeatedly starting sentences with "the," and the peer's suggestion of using longer sentences and bigger words does not address that specific pattern or add transitions showing how ideas connect.
hints: The lesson says a real fix does one of two specific things you can point at in the words. What are those two things?
Swapping words or adding length is not the same as removing repetition or stating a relationship. What would actually need to change in these five sentences to fix the choppy rhythm?

problemText: What does the removal test help you decide about a part of a sentence?
choices: Whether covering the words with your thumb shows that the part is essential to identify what the sentence is about or whether it adds extra description that could be removed
Whether the information is nonrestrictive and needs to be set off with matching marks, or restrictive and does not need commas
Whether a word is spelled correctly in the context of formal writing standards and usage conventions
Whether the sentence is written as a question, a statement, or an exclamatory form
hints: Think about what it means to cover a part of the sentence with your thumb and read what is left.
The test helps you figure out if the extra part changes what the sentence is talking about.

problemText: Jordan has three best friends. Which sentence correctly uses commas to show that "Alex" is extra information identifying one of those friends?
choices: Jordan's, best friend, Alex loves to skateboard on weekends.
Jordan's best friend, Alex, loves to skateboard on weekends.
Jordan's best friend Alex loves to skateboard on weekends.
Jordan's best friend, Alex loves to skateboard on weekends.
hints: When there are three friends, naming one of them tells you which friend is meant, so the name is necessary information.
Necessary information does not need commas—the sentence needs the name to identify the correct friend.

problemText: Mr. Park runs exactly one robotics club at the school. Use the removal test: if you cover the words "the robotics club," does the sentence "Mr. Park, the robotics club, meets on Thursdays" still point to the same thing? What does this tell you?
choices: No, it changes the meaning significantly, so the words are nonrestrictive and must have a comma placed before and after them to mark the information as removable
No, it changes the meaning because those words are the only way to identify what the sentence refers to, so they are restrictive and should not have any commas around them
Yes, it still points to Mr. Park correctly, so the words function as restrictive information that is essential to the sentence and should remain in place without any punctuation marks added
Yes, it still points to Mr. Park, so the words are nonrestrictive and should be set off with a matching pair of marks.
hints: Cover the words and ask: does the sentence still identify the exact same thing without them?
Since Mr. Park runs only one robotics club, the sentence can point to it just by saying 'Mr. Park' — so the club name is extra.

problemText: Read this sentence: "The book that won the award sits on the top shelf." The reader does not know which book is meant without the words "that won the award." After you run the removal test, what should you do to fix the punctuation, and why?
choices: Leave the sentence exactly as it is because this is restrictive information the sentence needs to identify the book.
Add a comma before "that" and after "award" because this is nonrestrictive information that needs to be set off.
Add a comma only after "award" because nonrestrictive information at the end needs one mark to set it off.
Add commas around the word "book" to make the sentence clearer for the reader.
hints: Cover the words 'that won the award' with your thumb. Can you still tell which book the sentence means without them?
If covering the words leaves the reader unsure which book is being talked about, the words are restrictive and the sentence needs them.

problemText: A student wrote: "My neighbor Mrs. Chen waters her garden every morning." The student has only one neighbor. The student wants to set off "Mrs. Chen" with a pair of dashes instead of commas but made a punctuation error. Which version fixes the mistake?
choices: My neighbor—Mrs. Chen waters her garden every morning.
My neighbor — Mrs. Chen — waters her garden every morning.
My neighbor, Mrs. Chen — waters her garden every morning.
My neighbor — Mrs. Chen, waters her garden every morning.
hints: When extra information sits in the middle of a sentence, you need a matching pair of the same mark—one before and one after.
Dashes are the same mark on both sides; never mix a dash with a comma to open and close the same extra information.

problemText: A writer has two sentences to punctuate. In the first, Emma has two sisters, and one of them is named Ava. In the second, the writer has exactly one pet, and its name is Whiskers. The writer says, "Sister Ava helped me study," and "My pet Whiskers ate all the treats." Without running the removal test on both, explain why only one of these sentences should have commas around the name, and rewrite the sentence that needs them.
choices: The first sentence needs commas: "Sister, Ava, helped me study." Both names are extra because the writer is talking to Emma and to the pet at the same time.
The second sentence needs commas: "My pet, Whiskers, ate all the treats." The name Whiskers is necessary to identify which pet, but the name Ava is extra because Emma has two sisters.
The first sentence needs commas: "Sister, Ava, helped me study." The name Ava is necessary to say which sister, but the name Whiskers is extra because the writer has only one pet.
Both sentences need commas because all names added to a sentence must be set off to show respect for the people and animals named.
hints: Run the removal test on each name separately. Ask: does the sentence still identify the exact same person or animal without the name?
When there are multiple sisters, naming one tells you which; when there is only one pet, the name just adds extra information.

problemText: Which of the following best describes what register means in writing? You are deciding what to write for a thank-you note to a teacher versus a text message to a friend.
choices: The set of rules governing punctuation marks, capitalization, and agreement between subjects and verbs in a written piece
The structural organization of a piece of writing, including how many paragraphs are needed and how sentences are arranged within them
How formal or informal a piece of writing needs to be for its audience and purpose
The central message or idea that a writer chooses to develop and support throughout an entire composition
hints: Think about what changes when you write to a teacher versus a friend—is it the topic, or something about how you phrase things?
Register is about the level of formality a writer chooses for one whole piece.

problemText: Read this student's email to the principal about a school event. Which sentence breaks the email's formal register? The email reads: "The Environmental Club would like to host an eco-friendly fair in the gym on Earth Day. We have already secured local vendors and organized our display stations. Honestly, the whole project is gonna be absolutely lit, and everyone should totally come. We are requesting permission to use the gym space from 9:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m."
choices: The Environmental Club would like to host an eco-friendly fair in the gym on Earth Day.
We are requesting permission to use the gym space from 9:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m.
We have already secured local vendors and organized our display stations.
Honestly, the whole project is gonna be absolutely lit, and everyone should totally come.
hints: Compare sentences to each other—which one uses casual words and slang that do not match the others?
Look for contractions, casual filler words, and exaggerated language that stand out from the rest of the piece.

problemText: Read this excerpt from a friend's letter about a weekend adventure. Which sentence breaks the letter's warm, casual tone? The letter reads: "We hiked up the mountain trail super early on Saturday morning, and honestly it was so worth it. The sunrise from the top was absolutely beautiful, and we got some amazing photos. The atmospheric conditions facilitated optimal visibility and photographic opportunities. Afterward, we stopped at our favorite diner for pancakes and didn't stop talking until we got home."
choices: The atmospheric conditions facilitated optimal visibility and photographic opportunities.
The sunrise from the top was absolutely beautiful, and we got some amazing photos.
We hiked up the mountain trail super early on Saturday morning, and honestly it was so worth it.
Afterward, we stopped at our favorite diner for pancakes and didn't stop talking until we got home.
hints: Which sentence sounds stiff and formal compared to the friendly, everyday tone of the other sentences?
Look for words like 'facilitated,' 'atmospheric conditions,' and 'optimal' that sound like they belong in a textbook, not a letter to a friend.

problemText: A student wrote this paragraph for a history assignment on colonial transportation: "Colonial merchants relied heavily on river routes to transport goods between settlements. Boats were the primary means of shipping everything from grain to textiles. Basically, rivers were like the highways of back then, which was pretty convenient for everyone. Roads were often muddy and impassable during winter months, making water transport essential for survival." The student needs to fix one sentence to match the paragraph's formal, informative register. Which revision best replaces the sentence that breaks the tone?
choices: Basically, rivers served as major trade routes, similar to modern highways in their importance to commerce.
Rivers functioned as crucial trade arteries, providing the most reliable transportation network in the colonial economy.
For real, rivers were super important back then because they were basically the only way to move stuff easily.
Anyway, everyone used rivers because roads were really bad and you could get stuck in the mud all the time.
hints: The fix must keep the same information about rivers' importance while matching the formal, informative tone of the rest of the paragraph.
Which choice uses precise vocabulary and formal transitions instead of casual filler words like 'basically' or 'pretty convenient'?

problemText: A student is revising a personal narrative about learning to ride a bike. The draft reads: "I was terrified when my dad first took off my training wheels. My heart was pounding so hard I thought it might explode out of my chest. The aforementioned psychological state of anxiety precipitated a moment of hesitation. But then I felt my dad's hand steadying the bike, and I just went for it." To fix this paragraph's consistency, the student must rewrite one sentence in the casual, warm register established by the others. Which sentence is the lapse, and what is one clear reason it breaks the tone?
choices: The lapse is 'I was terrified when my dad first took off my training wheels' because it tells the reader directly what the writer felt instead of showing the emotion through descriptive details and actions.

The lapse is 'My heart was pounding so hard I thought it might explode out of my chest' because it relies on figurative language and comparison, which creates distance from the genuine personal experience being shared.
The lapse is 'The aforementioned psychological state of anxiety precipitated a moment of hesitation' because it uses stiff, formal vocabulary and jargon that does not match the warm personal tone.

The lapse is 'But then I felt my dad's hand steadying the bike, and I just went for it' because it uses a series of actions rather than explaining the reasons behind the narrator's decision to proceed.
hints: Apply the procedure: read all sentences first to establish which register the majority use, then check each sentence against that majority.
The words 'aforementioned,' 'precipitated,' and 'psychological state of anxiety' are precise, formal language that stands out sharply from the rest.

problemText: A student wrote this restaurant review for a local blog: "The new taco place on Main Street has quickly become my favorite spot for lunch. The al pastor tacos are absolutely delicious, with perfectly seasoned pork and fresh pineapple. This culinary establishment demonstrates exceptional expertise in the application of traditional Mexican preparation techniques. The owner is friendly, the prices are reasonable, and I have already recommended it to all my friends." The student wants to maintain a warm, personal tone throughout. Identify which sentence breaks the consistency, explain why it breaks the tone, and describe what would make an effective revision.
choices: The sentence 'The new taco place on Main Street has quickly become my favorite spot for lunch' breaks the tone because it uses a location reference that sounds too much like a news report instead of a personal recommendation, and it should be rewritten to focus more on the writer's emotional connection to the place.

The sentence 'The al pastor tacos are absolutely delicious, with perfectly seasoned pork and fresh pineapple' breaks the tone because it shifts away from describing personal feelings and instead provides too many technical ingredient details that distance the reader from the genuine enthusiasm of the earlier sentences.

The sentence 'The owner is friendly, the prices are reasonable, and I have already recommended it to all my friends' breaks the tone because it suddenly becomes more structured and list-like rather than flowing naturally, making it feel disconnected from the warm, enthusiastic style established throughout most of the review.

The sentence 'This culinary establishment demonstrates exceptional expertise in the application of traditional Mexican preparation techniques' breaks the tone because it uses stiff, formal vocabulary and jargon instead of the conversational, personal language the rest of the review uses. A revision should describe the tacos in warm, everyday words while keeping the same message about their quality.
hints: Compare the vocabulary in each sentence to the vocabulary in the others—which sentence uses words that are noticeably more formal or technical than the rest?
A successful revision keeps the message (that the tacos are made with skill and care) but rewrites it in the casual, friendly tone established by the opening and closing sentences.
